messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: The paper presents PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format). In a 16-participant within-subjects lab study, prompts written with the template scored higher on an automatic task measure (0.74 vs. 0.61) and gave higher self-reported confidence, though they took slightly longer to write.

sections.title: What the authors built and tested
sections.text: The authors describe a four-slot editor (role, task, examples, output format) where each slot has a hint and an example, and the slots are assembled into one editable prompt with a preview. Participants completed three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, topic labelling, news summarisation) in both a free-form condition and the PromptScaffold condition.

sections.title: Main findings and their limits
sections.text: The authors report a higher mean task score with PromptScaffold, the largest gap on topic labelling, and higher confidence (4.1 vs. 3.4 on a 7-point scale), with time to final prompt rising from 6.2 to 7.5 minutes. The authors also note that the template did not teach participants why the slots matter, and that the sample was small, homogeneous and tested in one 70-minute session.

People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. messages.text: What are the limitations of this study?

messages.short_answer: The authors name four limitations: a small, homogeneous sample of 16 mostly computing university students, a single 70-minute lab session, only three predefined tasks with one LLM, and reliance on an automatic task score and self-reported confidence. For your user study, the main issues are who was sampled and which outcome measures were used.

sections.title: Limitations the authors state
sections.text: The authors list three main limitations: the sample was small and homogeneous, each participant used the tool in one session, and only three tasks and one LLM were tested. They also say success was measured only with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence.

sections.title: What these limits mean for a non-expert prompt study
sections.text: Because your study targets non-expert users, the sampling limit matters most: the authors' participants were university students, so you would need to decide how to recruit a broader population and report who you reached. The single-session design also means novelty effects could affect confidence, so you might plan a repeated or longer session if your research question concerns sustained use. Adding expert ratings of prompt quality and open-ended tasks, as the authors suggest, could help you judge whether the measures you choose really capture prompt quality.

sections.title: What could carry over to a study of non-expert prompt writing
sections.text: A free-form baseline, counterbalanced order and parallel task versions could help you separate the effect of a tool or support from the order of conditions and from repeated exposure to the same inputs. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. sections.title: What these limits mean for a non-expert prompt study
sections.text: Because your study targets non-expert users, the sampling limit matters most: the authors' participants were university students, so you would need to decide how to recruit a broader population and report who you reached. The single-session design also means novelty effects could affect confidence, so you might plan a repeated or longer session if your research question concerns sustained use. Adding expert ratings of prompt quality and open-ended tasks, as the authors suggest, could help you judge whether the measures you choose really capture prompt quality.

2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists.
